title: The Count at the Low Gate
passages:
The Stair shut behind them like a door in a house where nobody lived anymore, and after that it was the reach: six miles of drowned suburb with the squall stacked up black over the Kettle at the far end, close enough now that the swell came at them from astern instead of the side.

Bayo stood in the bow with his hands wrapped in strips torn off somebody's shirt, the burns showing through in two dark patches. Dey held the bow line for him, because Bayo couldn't.

"Stump, starboard bow, big as a bus."

"Got it."

"Roof," Bayo said. "Only a roof."

"There's never nothing under a roof," Dey said.

"Nineteen years I've called this reach and held my own line doing it." Bayo said it to the water, then turned and said it to the wheelhouse, loud, so it was on the record of everybody's ears. "Not anymore. My hands are done. I call water and nothing else from here, and you'll not have to guess at it later."

"Noted," Sol said, without looking round. "Keep calling."

Off the port quarter the old road ran down into the brown in long flat steps, each one a fathom, and where the steps quit there was the spoke-box — a traffic circle from before, eight arms of road still standing a hand's width proud of slack water. Wren lobbed the cork floats into it, two bark discs the size of saucers, and the whole deck watched which way the ebb took them.

"Coming back at us," she said.

"Then the hub's turning and we're on the wrong side of it." Bayo pointed with a bandaged finger, which was the most his hands could do. "Mid-channel. Take the middle and let the ebb carry you down."

"We go inside the red," Sol said.

"Inside the red is shoal."

"Inside the red is a fathom more water than the middle, and a fathom is what I'm buying." She put the wheel over. The Marrow leaned, the floats swept by the hull going the other way, and that was the argument finished. "Wren, get inboard of the frame."

Mara was lashed at the wrists in the lift-frame with her chin up, counting. "Sixty-one. Sixty-two." A pause, pleasant as weather. "Somebody's rope."

Nia stood at the rail with the orange wand held against her ribs, warming nothing, and her face went flat the way it did.

The low gate was an arch of poured concrete with a grate under it, forty feet of welded plate and rebar hanging on four chains, and the chains were paying out a notch at a time while the season bell in the tower above rang. Bayo counted the tolls, since counting was what he had instead of hands.

"Six. Three to a shutting."

"Boom," Sol said.

Dey hit the release and the cargo boom came down across the deck with a bang that went through the whole boat, and under the counter, below, Teo slept through it. They slid under the grate with the plate a foot above the wheelhouse, and the chains took another notch behind them, and outside the arch the reach turned white where the squall finally got to it.

Inside was a stone basin, a floating stage, one lantern on a pole. The dock-warden was already at the counter with the berth book open under her hand, and she did not wait for the bow line to be made fast.

"You're one short," Pru Quill said. "The book ends a soul short, and if it ends that way my own berth is forfeit. I'll not round it and I'll not sit on it till morning."

Quill hooked the lantern over the edge of the book to steady it, because the stage was moving on the swell and she was not going to write crooked.

"*Marrow.* Out of the Stair, in on the seventh toll." The pencil was a stub the length of her thumb, held in her fist like a knife. "Master."

"Sol Ferreira."

"Ferreira." She wrote it. "Diver."

"Dey Okafor," Dey said, chin up, like he was volunteering for something worse.

"Okafor." Write. "Topside."

"Wren Achebe."

The pencil stopped. "You're the slate reader."

"I rebuild hours," Wren said. "When people let me."

"Deckhand," Quill said, and Bayo said "Bayo Adisa" before she had finished asking. She wrote Bayo Adisa, then looked at the gap after it where a mark goes. "No mark."

"No mark," Bayo agreed, warm as a hand on your shoulder, like he was giving her something.

"There's a child below," Quill said. "I heard him breathing when your boom came down. I'll have him at this counter before I close."

"He's twelve and he's asleep," Nia said.

"Then he can wake up and be twelve here."

Past the arch the squall had gone from black to a grey with rain in it. Nobody looked at it twice. Quill turned to the last ruled line on the page.

"Name."

Mara had her chin up, watching the chains pay out. "Seventy-eight," she said. "Somebody's rope."

"Mara Vos," Nia said.

"Not off you." Quill didn't raise her voice. She'd no need. "The book takes a name out of the mouth it belongs to. Anything else is a rumour, and I don't write rumours."

"Seventy-nine." Then, to Nia, kindly, the way you'd answer a stranger who'd stopped you in the street to ask the way: "Is it your rope?"

Nia's jaw did something. Dey put a hand on her shoulder and she let him leave it there.

"Write it how she said it," Wren said. "Mara Vos. I'll stand to it. I've her daughter's slate, I've the Caller's spool, I've fourteen months of a man saying it in the dark—"

"Two of you can't hold one line. One soul, one line." The pencil did not move. "And I'll not take a name handed to me like a coat."

"Put mine against hers, then," Bayo said. "Surety. I'll sign for her keep."

"Surety's a debt. This book counts bodies, and a debt doesn't ride up in the cage."

"There's four hundred women in the Kettle," Dey said. "Write *woman*. That's accurate."

"It's a description. I had a description in this book once and it cost me a winter." She looked up, and she looked at Mara properly for the first time, the way you look at a knot you're going to have to pick out of a wet line. "I've no patience for a woman being coy with her own name, either. No name, no line. No line, nothing goes up out of this basin. Not a crate, not a chair, not her. She sits on my stage till the spring bell with the water coming up to the counter, and I will not invent her a name to save my own berth."

Salas stood at the frame with one hand on the rope. He hadn't spoken since the Stair. He didn't speak now.

The bell went. Inside the basin it came flat and doubled, off all that concrete, and above the arch the chain took its notch and the plate came down with a noise like a boiler settling. The gap of grey light under it went from a hand's width to less.

"Two gone," Bayo said. "One left in the chain."

"Eighty," Mara said, pleasant as weather. "Somebody's rope."
